clue.text: Well-known cook apostrophized by Cowper?

definitions.meaning: ... Smith is Britain's best-known television cookery writer
William Cowper addressed early love poems to his cousin Theadora under a pastoral name

explanation.surface: A celebrity chef turns out to have been the subject of an eighteenth-century poet's verses.
explanation.definitionFit: The same first name belongs to a famous British television cook and to the beloved Cowper's poems speak to directly.

clue.text: Spirit of social equality expressed by Henry Brooks Adams

definitions.meaning: the egalitarian principle of rule by the people
Henry Adams published an anonymous satirical novel about Washington politics with this title in 1880

explanation.surface: An American historian is credited with voicing the egalitarian spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the political ideal of equal popular rule and the title of Henry Adams's 1880 novel.

clue.text: Table reportedly showing Hungarian composer

indicators.note: reportedly tells us the word is heard rather than seen, so we take its sound

parts.note: a table of items is a list

explanation.surface: A table seems to reveal a Hungarian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' signals a homophone: LIST, a table, is said like the composer's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was the Romantic pianist-composer born in Hungary in 1811.

clue.text: Concerto consort

definitions.meaning: the so-called ... Concerto for violin, once attributed to the boy Mozart but in fact a twentieth-century pastiche
Queen ... was consort of the British king William IV

explanation.surface: Two words of music, as if a concerto were being played by a consort of viols.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consort' looks musical next to 'Concerto' (a consort of viols), but it means a royal spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a violin piece falsely credited to Mozart and to William IV's queen.

clue.text: Shakespeare's "Old Sir Thomas", who claimed to lie like a king

definitions.text: Shakespeare's "Old Sir Thomas", who claimed to lie like a king

parts.words: Shakespeare's "Old Sir Thomas", who claimed to lie like a king
parts.note: in Henry V the old knight tells the disguised king he may now say 'Now lie I like a king', meaning he sleeps well on the hard ground

explanation.surface: An old Shakespearean knight boasts that he can tell lies as royally as a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lie' suggests telling untruths, but the knight means lying down to sleep; the line comes from Henry V, Act 4.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Erpingham is the elderly officer whom Henry addresses as 'old Sir Thomas' on the eve of Agincourt.

clue.text: They shaded O'Neill's longing

parts.note: Eugene O'Neill's play title puts longing, that is Desire, beneath certain trees

explanation.surface: Something cast a shadow over a playwright's yearning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'longing' stands for Desire, and O'Neill's 1924 play is Desire Under the Elms.
explanation.definitionFit: The trees in O'Neill's title stand over the farmhouse, literally shading Desire.

clue.text: "But one half-of bread to this intolerable deal of sack!" (Henry IV, Part I)

definitions.text: "But one half-of bread to this intolerable deal of sack!" (Henry IV, Part I)

parts.words: "But one half-of bread to this intolerable deal of sack!" (Henry IV, Part I)
parts.note: Prince Hal's line on reading Falstaff's tavern bill, with the missing word being a small quantity worth a coin

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a gap, mocking Falstaff's bill of mostly wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver fills the gap in Hal's line: one halfpenny's worth of bread against vast amounts of sack, a sweet wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means the amount that a penny buys, here half that amount of bread.

clue.text: It was one for John Dos Passos

definitions.text: It was one for John Dos Passos

parts.words: It was one for John Dos Passos
parts.note: Dos Passos wrote a 1943 novel about a populist politician titled with this word followed by One

explanation.surface: Something was a single thing for an American novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads backwards from the title Number One: 'one' completes the novel's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dos Passos's second District of Columbia novel is called Number One, so the word was 'one' for him.

clue.text: Elizabeth Bowen's "little girl once seen in a lithograph" by Leopold Grant Moody

definitions.text: Elizabeth Bowen's "little girl once seen in a lithograph" by Leopold Grant Moody

parts.words: Elizabeth Bowen's "little girl once seen in a lithograph" by Leopold Grant Moody
parts.note: in Bowen's The House in Paris the boy Leopold sees the English child who shares the house with him in this way

explanation.surface: A girl from a Bowen novel is pictured as if from an old print.
explanation.walkthrough: Leopold Grant Moody is the boy in The House in Paris; the girl he meets there is Henrietta Mountjoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrietta is the eleven-year-old companion whom Leopold sizes up as a lithograph child in Bowen's novel.

clue.text: Historical novelist in secret society? ()

definitions.meaning: A. E. W. ... wrote historical adventures such as The Four Feathers
a member of the Freemasons, the secretive fraternal order

explanation.surface: A writer of historical fiction is suspected of belonging to a secret society.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the author of The Four Feathers is also the short name for a Freemason, member of a sworn brotherhood.

clue.text: Marryat's mariner was "seldom at a loss" ("prepared" his second name)

definitions.text: Marryat's mariner was "seldom at a loss" ("prepared" his second name)

parts.words: Marryat's mariner was "seldom at a loss" ("prepared" his second name)
parts.note: Captain Marryat's novel title gives a seaman's first name before a surname meaning prepared

explanation.surface: A Marryat sailor is resourceful, and his surname confirms he is always ready.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel is Masterman Ready (1841); 'prepared' points at Ready, leaving the first name to enter.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterman Ready is the old sailor of Marryat's castaway novel, as resourceful as his name implies.

clue.text: He must die, wrote Mary Renault

definitions.text: He must die, wrote Mary Renault

parts.words: He must die, wrote Mary Renault
parts.note: Renault's novel The King Must Die retells Theseus's journey to Crete and its ruler

explanation.surface: A novelist declares that a man has to perish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' is the king of Renault's title The King Must Die: the Cretan ruler Theseus overthrows.
explanation.definitionFit: Minos is the Cretan monarch whose fall closes Renault's novel about Theseus.

clue.text: The old china gives feed to pet

parts.note: a cat is a typical household pet
hay is animal feed

explanation.surface: Someone feeds hay to the family cat, along with talk of antique porcelain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'china' looks like porcelain but means the country: Cathay is its old name.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathay is the medieval European name for the Chinese empire.

clue.text: Titanic work of Holderlin

parts.note: Hölderlin's epistolary novel is named after one of the Titans of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A huge achievement by the German poet Hölderlin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titanic' seems to mean enormous, but it means named after a Titan.
explanation.definitionFit: Hölderlin's 1797 novel bears the name of the Titan father of the sun.

clue.text: Hypocritical characteristic of Shakespeare, according to Dryden

definitions.meaning: two-faced, showing one face and hiding another

definitions.text: characteristic of Shakespeare, according to Dryden
definitions.meaning: Dryden praised Shakespeare as able to look both ways, like the Roman god of doorways with two faces

explanation.surface: Dryden judged Shakespeare a hypocrite.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-faced deceit and the double outlook Dryden found in Shakespeare share the image of the double-headed Roman god.

clue.text: Like Trollope's Grantly, he may aspire to see

definitions.text: Like Trollope's Grantly, he may aspire to see

parts.words: Like Trollope's Grantly, he may aspire to see
parts.note: in the Barchester novels Dr Grantly is a senior cleric hoping to become a bishop, a see being a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: Someone like a Trollope character hopes to catch sight of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' is not vision but a bishop's seat; Grantly in Barchester Towers hopes for his father's bishopric.
explanation.definitionFit: Grantly holds the office just below bishop in the Church of England, so promotion to a diocese is his ambition.

clue.text: Nerves act unpredictably for novelist

indicators.note: acting unpredictably means the letters behave erratically and land in a new order

explanation.surface: A novelist's nerves behave erratically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unpredictably' rearranges the letters of NERVES ACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Cervantes is the Spanish author of Don Quixote.

clue.text: Blow for Bram Stoker characters flying back

indicators.note: the creatures are made to fly in reverse, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: bats are the creatures Dracula turns into in Stoker's novel

explanation.surface: A blow is struck as Dracula's bats flutter backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying back' reverses BATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stab is a thrust with a blade, a kind of blow.

clue.text: Rare poet identified with every man

definitions.meaning: his epitaph in Westminster Abbey reads 'O rare' before his name
he wrote the comedy Every Man in His Humour

explanation.surface: An unusual poet is identified with everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jacobean dramatist is both the poet of the famous 'O rare' epitaph and the author of Every Man in His Humour.

clue.text: Badly written reel irks violinist

indicators.note: letters written badly come out jumbled, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: A violinist is annoyed by a poorly composed reel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly written' rearranges REEL IRKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fritz Kreisler was the Austrian-born virtuoso violinist and composer.

clue.text: Thread of story

definitions.meaning: spun fibre used in knitting or weaving

explanation.surface: The thread of a story.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both spun fibre and a rambling tale, from sailors spinning tales as they worked rope.

clue.text: Haggard hero may reveal strange antique ram

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters are made odd, i.e. rearranged

explanation.surface: A careworn hero comes upon an odd old ram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' looks like 'worn out' but is the novelist H. Rider Haggard; 'strange' rearranges ANTIQUE RAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Allan Quatermain is the hunter-adventurer of Rider Haggard's King Solomon's Mines.

clue.text: Gypsy cheat conceals cupid's friend

indicators.note: the phrase conceals the answer inside its run of letters

explanation.surface: A Gypsy cheat hides a friend of Cupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceals' means the answer is inside gyPSY CHEat.
explanation.definitionFit: Psyche is the mortal girl loved by Cupid in the myth told by Apuleius.

clue.text: "Oh, the Germans —, but the French arrange!" (Willa Cather)

definitions.text: "Oh, the Germans —, but the French arrange!" (Willa Cather)

parts.words: "Oh, the Germans —, but the French arrange!" (Willa Cather)
parts.note: Cather contrasts German systematic sorting with French artistic arranging; the gap is a verb for sorting into categories

explanation.surface: A Cather quotation with a gap, contrasting German and French habits of order.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is a verb opposed to 'arrange': to sort into types, the German way.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort things into categories is the methodical habit Cather attributes to the Germans.

clue.text: Record-breaking cricketer starts with a hundred for R. D. Blackmore's heroine

indicators.note: the cricketer starts with the other piece placed before him

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
Brian Lara of the West Indies holds the record for the highest Test innings

explanation.surface: A record-setting batsman begins with a century, and a Victorian heroine appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts with' puts C, the Roman hundred, before LARA, the West Indian batsman whose 400 not out is the Test record.
explanation.definitionFit: Clara Vaughan is the title heroine of Blackmore's first novel.

clue.text: Paisiello's barber

parts.note: Paisiello's opera Il barbiere di Siviglia predates Rossini's and has the same title character

explanation.surface: A barber who works for the composer Paisiello.
explanation.walkthrough: Paisiello set Beaumarchais's Barber of Seville in 1782, before Rossini.
explanation.definitionFit: Figaro is the scheming barber at the centre of Beaumarchais's comedy and Paisiello's opera.

clue.text: V. S. Naipaul's revolutionary starts a hostile movement (even dangerous) (.)

indicators.note: starts means the first letter of each following word is taken

explanation.surface: A Naipaul rebel begins a hostile and perhaps dangerous movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the first letters of A HOSTILE MOVEMENT EVEN DANGEROUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Jimmy Ahmed is the would-be guerrilla leader of Naipaul's novel Guerrillas.

clue.text: International organization, with hesitation, suggests one (out of many in the US?)

definitions.text: one (out of many in the US?)

parts.note: UN is the United Nations
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A hesitant United Nations hints at one among many in America.
explanation.walkthrough: The US motto e pluribus unum means 'out of many, one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unum is Latin for one, as in the American motto on the Great Seal.

clue.text: Witty salt

parts.note: the classical phrase for refined Athenian wit pairs salt with an adjective meaning Athenian

explanation.surface: A clever old sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salt' seems to be a sailor, but the clue points at the phrase for elegant wit, Attic salt, Attic meaning of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic describes the polished, pointed style of Athens, as in the phrase for delicate wit.

clue.text: Season suggesting road covered by George Mac Donald Fraser

definitions.meaning: the February church feast of the Purification, also a Scottish quarter day

definitions.text: suggesting road covered by George Mac Donald Fraser
definitions.meaning: Fraser's 1993 Border novel adds the word Road to this name

explanation.surface: A time of year hints at a road a novelist wrote about.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both the 2 February church festival and the first word of Fraser's novel Candlemas Road.

clue.text: Location of 11 of McEwan's Booker book

definitions.text: Location of 11 of McEwan's Booker book

parts.words: Location of 11 of McEwan's Booker book
parts.note: Ian McEwan's Booker-winning novel of 1998 is named after the Dutch city where its climax takes place

explanation.surface: A setting in McEwan's Booker-winning novel.
explanation.walkthrough: McEwan won the 1998 Booker with the novel named after the Dutch capital, where its two friends meet their end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch capital is both the title and the closing setting of McEwan's prize-winning novella.

clue.text: Pole with fashionable following was a sculptor

indicators.note: following means the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: a rod is a pole
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A Polish man with a stylish set of followers turned out to be a sculptor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish man but means a stick; 'following' is the charade signal, and 'was' is a link joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin was the French sculptor of The Thinker.
